idiom_name: pthread_once / C11 call_once guard around an init function
implementation_notes: C has no constructors for objects with static storage duration and no specified order for initializing them across translation units, so the classic structure has to be written by hand: keep the object in file scope, expose one accessor, and protect the check-and-build step with pthread_once (POSIX) or C11 call_once, which exist precisely as 'dynamic package initialization' for multi-threaded libraries (the POSIX rationale shows the unsynchronized flag idiom they replace). The per-translation-unit guard and counter of the nifty idiom has no standard equivalent: if a header-defined object must be alive before main, or before other units' initializers run, you need the non-portable GCC/Clang __attribute__((constructor)) or a linker-section (.init_array) trick, which re-introduces an unspecified order among constructors. Use pthread_once for ordinary first use and reserve constructor attributes for pre-main compatibility cases; the simpler alternative on plain C is an explicit init function called from main.
pitfalls: pthread_once's init routine must not recursively call pthread_once with the same once_control: the recursive call returns without running the initializer, so the outer call never completes (the POSIX page spells out this deadlock); jumping out of the init routine with longjmp makes the behaviour undefined.

There is no portable pre-main hook: __attribute__((constructor)) and .init_array are compiler and platform specifics, and they give no ordering guarantee across translation units, so they postpone rather than solve the order problem.
C11 <threads.h> is not universally available (glibc only gained it in 2.28), which is why pthread_once - POSIX, not ISO C - is the usual choice.
A failing initializer has no exception channel: unless init_obj records an error, obj_get returns whatever partial state the init function left behind.
